common_name: Ruby Bells Coral Bells (Classic Red-Flowered Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this older Heuchera sanguinea-type selection prefers a bit more sun than modern foliage hybrids as long as soil moisture is consistent.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, tolerating more sun in cooler climates if moisture stays consistent. Ruby Bells is a long-standing Heuchera sanguinea-type selection prized for wiry stems that carry vivid ruby-red, bell-shaped flowers well above the scalloped green foliage mound, making it a reliable hummingbird draw over a long early-summer bloom season. Shear spent flower stems to encourage rebloom and to keep the low mound looking tidy through summer. Divide congested clumps every three years in spring to maintain vigor and flower count.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Stormy Seas Coral Bells (Giant Ruffled Pewter-Purple Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this Heuchera villosa selection tolerates far more heat and humidity than micrantha-type cultivars, making it a strong choice for southern gardens.

directions: Site in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving afternoon shade where summers run hot. Stormy Seas produces an unusually large mound of heavily ruffled, pewter-purple leaves with a silvery overlay and dark charcoal veining, part of Terra Nova's heat-tolerant villosa breeding line developed for southern gardens where thinner-leaved coral bells struggle. Foliage color deepens with cooler fall temperatures, and the plant is grown primarily for its bold texture rather than its modest sprays of small white flowers. Refresh the mound by dividing every three to four years once the crown becomes congested.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Sashay Coral Bells (Deeply Ruffled Purple Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; like other villosa-type cultivars, Sashay handles summer heat and humidity better than micrantha hybrids.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to light shade, watering during dry spells to keep leaf edges from browning. Sashay carries deep purple leaves with pronounced wavy, ruffled margins that catch the light and move visibly in a breeze, giving the cultivar its name. As a Heuchera villosa selection it shrugs off summer humidity that can cause crown rot in thinner-leaved types, making it dependable in warm-summer regions. Mulch lightly in winter in the northern part of its range and divide clumps every three years to keep the ruffled foliage dense.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Vienna Coral Bells (Silvered Purple Ruffled-Leaf Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; part of a Terra Nova city-named series that also includes Paris and Binoche.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, protecting from harsh midday sun in warmer zones. Vienna forms a tidy mound of ruffled purple leaves overlaid with a silvery sheen and fine dark veining, sharing the same Terra Nova breeding line as the similarly styled Paris and Binoche cultivars. The metallic foliage effect is most pronounced in spring and fall when temperatures are cool. Divide every three to four years in early spring as the crown becomes woody and elevated above the soil line.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Persian Carpet Coral Bells (Patterned Metallic Purple Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; deeply lobed leaves show best color when grown in bright shade rather than deep shade.

directions: Site in well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright partial shade for the strongest foliage coloring. Persian Carpet earns its name from deeply lobed, intricately patterned leaves in metallic purple with a silver overlay and contrasting dark veins that read almost like a woven textile from a distance. Grown primarily as a foliage plant, it produces modest sprays of small cream flowers on wiry stems in late spring. Keep soil evenly moist and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain the dense, patterned mound.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Amethyst Myst Coral Bells (Silvery Amethyst-Purple Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the misty silver overlay develops most fully once plants are established and temperatures moderate in fall.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, avoiding hot afternoon sun that can bleach the delicate coloring. Amethyst Myst produces rounded, ruffled leaves in a soft amethyst-purple washed with a hazy silver sheen and fine dark venation, giving the mound a misted, smoky appearance rather than a hard metallic one. Small white flowers appear on slender stems in early summer but are secondary to the foliage display. Divide every three to four years in spring once the crown becomes crowded.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Snowstorm Coral Bells (Classic White-Marbled Variegated Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; the reduced chlorophyll in the cream-marbled leaves makes this older variegated cultivar less vigorous and more prone to scorch than green-leaved types.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltering from direct afternoon sun that quickly scorches its variegated leaves. Snowstorm is a long-grown Heuchera sanguinea selection with green leaves heavily marbled and splashed in cream-white, topped by wiry stems of small coral-red bell flowers in late spring. Because the pale sectors carry less chlorophyll, plants grow more slowly and need more consistent moisture than solid-green coral bells. Divide only when clumps become crowded, since this cultivar resents frequent disturbance more than modern hybrids.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; darkest leaf color develops in cooler weather and can green slightly during peak summer heat.

directions: Site in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade for the deepest, glossiest color. Blackout is among the darkest coral bells available, holding nearly jet-black, glossy rounded leaves through spring and fall, with color that can soften slightly to a deep charcoal-purple during the hottest weeks of summer. Its low, dense mound makes an effective dark accent against silver- or chartreuse-leaved companions in mixed shade plantings. Divide every three to four years in early spring to keep the clump vigorous and the crown from rising too far above soil level.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Pinot Gris Coral Bells (Pewter-Silver Ruffled Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; part of a wine-named Terra Nova color group prized for pewter and silver tones.

directions: Grow in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where the cool pewter-silver leaf tones are most pronounced. Pinot Gris produces ruffled, rounded leaves in soft silver-gray with faint underlying purple tones and darker veining, providing a muted, sophisticated foil for brighter-colored perennials nearby. Leaf color intensifies as nights cool in fall. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain a full, well-shaped mound.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Melting Fire Coral Bells (Fiery New-Growth Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; as a villosa-type selection it tolerates heat and humidity better than micrantha hybrids, similar to Fire Alarm and Fire Chief.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving afternoon shade in hot climates to prolong color intensity. Melting Fire emerges with vivid orange-red new growth at the leaf edges that gradually softens into an olive-bronze center as leaves mature, so each mound shows several colors at once. As a Heuchera villosa selection it handles summer heat and humidity notably better than micrantha-derived cultivars, making it a good choice for southern gardens. Divide every three to four years in spring once the clump becomes crowded.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
